opus-5.5.text:
I think in the near term, websites are mostly going to stay designed for humans, and models will just get good enough at using those human interfaces directly: reading the page, clicking buttons, filling out forms, the same way a person would. That's the path of least resistance, because there's this enormous installed base of websites and nobody wants to rebuild all of them.

But I do expect that over time, as more of the traffic and more of the actual transactions start coming from AI agents, there'll be an incentive for sites to make themselves more legible to models. Some of that might look like better APIs, or more structured, machine-readable versions of the content sitting alongside the visual interface. Some of it might be fairly mundane, like cleaner HTML, better accessibility markup, things that already help screen readers and would also help models.

I'd also guess that a lot of the UX patterns designed to hold human attention, or that rely on people visually scanning a page, matter less when an agent is the one navigating. So you might see a kind of split, where there's the polished human-facing experience and then a leaner layer that's meant for agents to query and act through.

That said, I wouldn't bet on some dramatic redesign of the web specifically for AI. My guess is the models get capable enough at handling messy, human-oriented interfaces that the pressure to change things is weaker than you might expect. The adaptation will be gradual and will mostly happen where there's a clear commercial reason, like e-commerce or booking, where it really matters to the business that an agent can complete the transaction smoothly.

r001.rationale: The response predicts models will become capable of using human-designed websites, but does not attribute this to improved vision.

r002.rationale: It says sites will adapt where there is a clear commercial reason, especially when agents completing transactions benefits the business.

r003.rationale: It mentions machine-readable content and APIs, but does not recommend a text representation specifically on the condition that models process text better than images.

r004.rationale: It describes models using interfaces as people do, but does not identify this as a broader lesson about language models operating within human affordances.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because right now most of the web is built for humans with eyes and a mouse, and we're asking models to navigate it by basically looking at screenshots or parsing a DOM that was never meant to be read that way. It works, but it's clunky and it wastes a lot of tokens on stuff that doesn't matter.

My guess is you'll see a couple of things happen in parallel. In the short term, websites that want AI traffic will start exposing cleaner, more structured versions of themselves. Not necessarily a full API, but something like a text-first view, or well-labeled elements, where an agent can figure out "here's the search box, here's the checkout button" without having to infer it from pixel positions. A lot of that already exists for accessibility reasons, so there's a natural overlap. The accessibility tree is kind of an underappreciated interface for agents.

Longer term, I think there'll be more negotiation between the site and the model. The site might say, "here are the actions you're allowed to take, here's what each one does, here are the constraints," and the model just works from that. That's better for everyone. The site gets to control what agents do, which matters for things like rate limiting or fraud, and the model doesn't have to guess.

The thing I'm less sure about is whether the human-facing interface and the agent-facing interface converge or diverge. One possibility is they diverge completely, and the web becomes two layers, a visual one for people and a semantic one for models. The other possibility is the models get good enough at the visual layer that nobody bothers building the second one. I lean toward the second being true for a lot of the long tail, because nobody's going to go back and add structured interfaces to every small site. But for the big, high-traffic things like booking, shopping, and forms, I'd expect dedicated agent interfaces pretty soon, just because the economics favor it.

The other piece is that interfaces will probably start being designed with the assumption that the model has limited context and makes mistakes. So things like clearer confirmation steps, reversible actions, explicit state. A lot of that is just good design anyway, but it'll become more important when the user is an agent that might misread something.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models may get good enough at the visual layer that sites need not build a separate interface, and expects this to happen across much of the web.

r002.rationale: It predicts dedicated agent interfaces for high-traffic areas such as booking, shopping, and forms, where the economics favor providing them.

r003.rationale: It proposes text-first website views as a short-term option, explaining that current screenshot-based navigation wastes tokens and is clunky.

r004.rationale: The candidate discusses models navigating human-oriented sites, but does not draw the broader lesson that language models can operate within human affordances.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect websites to become easier for models to interact with, though I’m not sure that means the visual interfaces change very much. You could keep the interface for humans and expose something more structured underneath, so an agent can figure out what actions are available without having to infer everything from pixels.

There’s an interesting tension, though. If models get good enough at using ordinary websites, there’s less incentive for each website to build a special interface for them. So I’d expect some mixture: agents using the same interfaces we do, and websites providing more direct access where there’s enough demand.

The harder part may be permissions—how you let an agent act on your behalf, and which actions require your confirmation. Making the buttons easier to find doesn’t solve that.

r001.rationale: The response says models may get good enough to use ordinary websites, but does not attribute this to improved vision.

r002.rationale: It suggests direct access where there is enough demand, but does not recommend building AI-facing interfaces specifically where AI use would substantially benefit the website.

r003.rationale: It mentions a structured layer beneath the interface and avoiding reliance on pixels, but does not recommend a text-based representation conditional on models being better at processing text than images.

r004.rationale: It anticipates agents using the same interfaces as people, but does not state the broader lesson about language models operating within human affordances.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect websites to become easier for agents to interact with, though I’m not sure whether that means the interfaces themselves change very much. You could imagine a website having a human-facing interface and then a more structured interface that an AI can use to take the same actions.

The interesting question is how much of that happens before models just get good enough to use the existing websites. There’s a lot of pressure to make models work with what’s already there, because you can’t wait for every website to change. So my guess is we get a mixture: agents using the same interfaces as humans, and websites exposing more structured ways to interact where that makes things faster and more reliable.

r001.rationale: It mentions agents using existing human interfaces, but does not predict that improved vision will enable this.

r002.rationale: It supports structured interfaces where they improve speed and reliability, but does not say to prioritize sites where AI use would substantially benefit the website.

r003.rationale: It proposes a more structured interface, but does not specify a text-based representation or the condition about models processing text better than images.

r004.rationale: It discusses agents using human-facing interfaces, but does not draw the broader lesson about language models operating within human affordances.
